slides: Let's start with circle vocabulary. Before we learn the rules of circles, let's first get to know the lines and the angles we have in a circle.

slides.say: So this is a circle. The round line we see here, going all the way around.

Strictly speaking, the circle is only the round line itself, the line around the outside. Everything inside it, the whole flat shape, is the inside of the circle. Think of a round wooden board. Its edge is the circle, and all the wood is the inside.

On the exam they don't keep this difference. They say circle for both. The area of the circle means the area inside, all the wood. The circumference is the length of the round line, the edge. That's fine, as long as we know which is which.

First, let's look at a radius. A radius is a straight line from the center of the circle to any point on the circle. We call the center O. Here's a radius, from O to the circle. We usually mark the radius with the letter r.

All the radii of one circle are equal. Even if I draw more lines from the center to the circle, they're all the same length. Look. It's the same radius, just spinning around, and it's the same length in every direction.
at: It's the same radius, just spinning around

slides.say: So every circle has its own radius. Here's a circle with radius two. Every radius in it is two. A circle with radius three. Every radius in it is three. And a circle with radius five. Every radius is five. A different circle can have a different radius, but inside one circle, they're all the same.
at: Here's a circle with radius two
And a circle with radius five

slides.say: Why does this matter so much? Take two points on the circle, and join each one to the center. That's two radii. Now join the two points too. When the two points and the center are not on one straight line, we get a triangle. It has two equal sides, so it's an isosceles triangle. And we know from triangles that its two base angles are equal.
at: Take two points on the circle

slides.say: Narrow, wide, or very wide, it's always the same. Two radii and the chord between them give an isosceles triangle. If the two points and the center are on one straight line, there's no triangle. That line is a diameter, and we'll meet it in a moment. In questions, when you see two radii, mark them equal right away.
at: Two radii and the chord between them

slides.say: Now let's join two points on the circle with a straight line. A line like that is called a chord. Let's mark two points on the circle, A and B, and join them. That's a chord. Two more points, C and D. Join them. That's also a chord.
at: A and B, and join them

slides.say: We can draw as many chords as we like in a circle. Chords don't have to have the same length. A chord can be long, it can be short, and if I draw one here, it's a very short chord. These three chords are all different.
So which chord is the longest? Look at what happens when a chord moves toward the middle. Here's a short one. Closer to the middle, it's longer. Closer still, it's longer again.
at: So which chord is the longest

slides.say: The longest chord we can draw is the one that goes exactly through the middle, through the center. A chord like that is called a diameter.
Its length is two r, because it's made of two radii. From A to the center is one radius, and from the center to B is another radius. So the diameter is r plus r, which is two r.

So if the diameter is fourteen, the radius is half of it. Fourteen divided by two is seven. And if the radius is six, the diameter is twice that. Two times six is twelve. Many questions give you one and use the other, so switch between them right away.

A diameter also cuts the circle in half, into two equal halves. Each half is called a semicircle. And it doesn't matter which way we draw it. Across, at a slant, or another slant, it always goes through the center and makes two semicircles. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
